PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: November 7, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026342 The impact of international financial reporting standards adoption and the moderating role of blockchain technology on earnings management: A case study of nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam Thi Ngoc Diep Nguyena | Thi Hoang Yen Vub aHo Chi Minh City Open University, Vietnam. bVNU University of Economics and Business, Vietnam National University, Hanoi, Vietnam. Abstract This study investigates the impact of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) adoption on earnings management and examines the moderating role of blockchain technology in this relationship within the context of Vietnam's emerging market, as the country navigates its voluntary IFRS adoption phase (2022–2025). To achieve this, the study employs a quantitative, cross-sectional design, utilizing both primary and secondary data from 218 nonfinancial listed companies. Primary data on the extent of IFRS and blockchain adoption were gathered via structured surveys administered to chief financial officers and chief accountants, while secondary financial data from 2022–2024 were used to measure earnings management through the modified Jones model. Hierarchical regression analysis was conducted to test the research hypotheses. The findings reveal that IFRS adoption has a significant negative effect on earnings management, suggesting that adherence to international standards constrains opportunistic reporting behavior. More importantly, blockchain technology not only directly reduces earnings management but also significantly strengthens the negative relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management, indicating that the effectiveness of IFRS in curbing earnings management is more pronounced in firms with higher levels of blockchain implementation. These findings are significant as they demonstrate that regulatory reform (IFRS) is more effective when complemented by technological innovation (blockchain). Practically, this implies that managers should pursue coordinated investments in both IFRS compliance and blockchain systems to maximize reporting quality. For policymakers in Vietnam, the research provides evidence for integrating technological readiness into the mandatory IFRS adoption roadmap. The study's novelty lies in its integrated approach, as it is one of the first in Vietnam to empirically test the synergistic interaction between a regulatory standard and a disruptive technology, thereby providing a theoretical framework and empirical evidence for the complementary roles of regulation and technology in enhancing financial reporting integrity. Keywords: blockchain technology, earnings management, financial reporting quality, IFRS adoption 1. Introduction Over the past decade, global financial markets have undergone a significant shift toward the standardization of financial reporting practices through the widespread adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), which are currently implemented in more than 160 countries. This harmonization of accounting standards represents a fundamental change toward greater transparency, comparability, and reliability in corporate financial reporting. For developing economies such as Vietnam, the transition to IFRS is not merely a technical adjustment but also a strategic approach to enhance integration with global capital markets and financial systems (Nguyen et al., 2023; Tran, 2021). Vietnam's approach to IFRS adoption is characterized by clear, targeted planning and phased implementation. In March 2020, the Ministry of Finance issued Decision No. 345/QD-BTC, establishing a roadmap that includes a preparatory phase (2020- 2021), a voluntary adoption phase (2022-2025), and a mandatory implementation phase beginning in 2025. The transition from Vietnamese accounting standards (VASs) to IFRSs marked a significant milestone in the country's economic development and international financial integration (Ministry of Finance, 2020). Studies suggest that IFRS implementation can enhance the quality of financial reporting information, attract foreign investment, improve international competitiveness, promote business efficiency, and more accurately reflect firm value Multidiscip. Additionally, the adoption of international standards can reduce the costs associated with developing national accounting frameworks and accelerate their integration into the global financial system (Hung, 2022). However, this transition also faces certain hurdles due to Vietnam's unique political and economic context— marked by its transition from a centrally planned economy to a socialist-oriented market economy—which poses obstacles to effective IFRS implementation (Nguyen, 2022). Although IFRS adoption offers significant advantages to stakeholders, the issue of earnings management within enterprises remains a challenge even with IFRS in place. Earnings management refers to the manipulation of financial statements by managers to meet internal targets or external expectations, often at the expense of transparency and accuracy of financial information and market efficiency (Healy & Wahlen, 1999). While IFRS is designed to enhance reporting quality through its principles-based framework, it also allows for managerial discretion in applying accounting estimates and judgments, which can be exploited as an opportunity for information manipulation. Empirical evidence from both developed and emerging markets shows mixed results regarding the effectiveness of IFRS in mitigating earnings management. For instance, Capkun et al. (2016) argue that while IFRS adoption improves comparability, it does not consistently reduce discretionary accruals, especially in environments with weak enforcement mechanisms. In Vietnam, the institutional framework and legal corridors for accounting and auditing are still incomplete, and weak corporate governance undermines the benefits of IFRS adoption. According to Pham (2022) and Hung (2025), Vietnamese listed companies exhibit evidence of earnings management through discretionary accruals, particularly before and during equity offerings. Vo & Bui (2017) reported that firms with poor governance structures are more likely to engage in earnings management even amidst regulatory reforms. Therefore, adopting IFRS alone, without complementary mechanisms, may not be sufficient to curb financial statement manipulation. This phenomenon highlights the complex interplay between regulatory frameworks and managerial discretion in financial reporting (Leuz et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2010). The modified Jones model has become a widely accepted tool for detecting discretionary accruals, serving as a proxy for earnings management. This model improves upon previous approaches by accounting for the potential manipulation of revenue through credit sales to customers, thereby providing a more accurate measure of earnings management activities (Dechow et al., 1995). This reality necessitates the integration of innovative tools that can enhance the enforcement and monitoring of corporate financial disclosures. One such tool is blockchain technology. Blockchain is a decentralized ledger system that ensures data immutability, transparency, and real-time transaction tracking (Dai & Vasarhelyi, 2017). Its application in accounting and auditing has the potential to mitigate the risk of financial manipulation by creating a shared, tamper-proof record of transactions. Yermack (2017) hypothesizes that blockchain could revolutionize corporate governance by enhancing the reliability and auditability of corporate disclosures. In Vietnam, blockchain has been identified as a key pillar in the National Digital Transformation Program, and its adoption is gradually expanding in sectors such as banking, logistics, and fintech (Ministry of Information and Communications, 2020; Hung & Que, 2024). However, its role in financial reporting, particularly its regulatory impact on earnings management, remains underexplored. While IFRS adoption theoretically promotes financial reporting quality and mitigates earnings management, empirical evidence from developing countries shows inconsistent results. Studies by Sellami & Fakhfakh (2013) document varying impacts of IFRS implementation on earnings management practices across different institutional contexts. It is often moderated by factors such as enforcement mechanisms and corporate governance structures (Ball, 2006; Soderstrom & Sun, 2007). Specifically, in Vietnam, Pham et al. (2021) reported that while overall reporting quality improved following Vietnamese accounting reforms, earnings manipulation persisted significantly, suggesting that regulatory reforms alone may be insufficient. The ability of IFRS to curb earnings management heavily depends on the quality of implementation and the presence of supporting mechanisms. Research in emerging markets has indicated that IFRS adoption might lead to changes in earnings management strategies rather than their elimination, with firms potentially substituting real earnings management for accrual- based earnings management. This substitution effect suggests the limitations of relying solely on accounting standards to enhance financial reporting integrity (Chen et al., 2010; Zang, 2012). Furthermore, studies on the integration of digital governance tools with financial reporting frameworks are limited. Although blockchain technology has garnered considerable attention in finance research, empirical investigations linking blockchain adoption to financial reporting quality remain scarce (Tiberius & Hirth, 2019). Previous research has predominantly examined the separate links between IFRS and earnings management and between blockchain and earnings management, with few studies exploring the integrated impact of blockchain on the relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management. This is particularly evident in Vietnam, where both IFRS and blockchain adoption are relatively new phenomena (Nguyen, 2022). Moreover, as Vietnam implements its IFRS adoption roadmap, understanding the combined effects of IFRS and digital technology becomes increasingly critical for policymakers, regulators, and business leaders. While blockchain adoption in Vietnam is still nascent, there is growing recognition of its potential benefits in accounting and auditing (Nguyen et al., 2023). The uniqueness of this study lies in its integration of both regulatory (IFRS adoption) and technological (blockchain adoption) dimensions to investigate their combined impact on earnings management, an area that has received limited https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 3 attention in developing countries. While prior studies have often focused on the individual effects of IFRS adoption on earnings management (e.g., Barth et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2013) or explored the general impact of blockchain technology on accounting transparency and efficiency (e.g., Yermack, 2017; Dai & Vasarhelyi, 2017), our research is among the first in Vietnam to employ a direct moderation analysis to understand how blockchain technology adoption influences the relationship between IFRS implementation and earnings management practices within nonfinancial listed firms. Specifically, this study employs a quantitative methodology, leveraging both primary survey data and secondary financial statement analysis to assess not only the direct impact of IFRS adoption but also the interactive effect of IFRS with blockchain adoption on earnings management. By doing so, our research moves beyond traditional pre- and post-adoption comparisons of accounting standards (as seen in previous Vietnamese studies, e.g., Nguyen et al., 2023) and instead focuses on the concurrent technological and regulatory environment shaping Vietnam's corporate sector. This approach allows us to contribute to the ongoing debate on how digital transformation, particularly through blockchain, can reinforce or even supersede the regulatory benefits of international accounting standards in curbing earnings management. Our findings offer significant insights for both policymakers and auditors—tasked with designing and enforcing effective regulatory frameworks in a rapidly changing digital economy—as well as for managers of nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam, who must navigate the dual challenges of compliance and innovation. Ultimately, this study offers practical recommendations for leveraging blockchain technology to maximize the transparency and integrity of financial reporting in the Vietnamese context. Therefore, on the basis of the identified research gap and Vietnam's specific financial reporting environment, this study aims to achieve three primary objectives: (i) First, to examine the impact of IFRS adoption on earnings management among nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam. By focusing on the voluntary adoption phase (2022–2025), this study will provide timely insights into how the transition from VAS to IFRS affects firms' financial reporting behavior and earnings quality, using the modified Jones model to measure discretionary accruals. (ii) Second, to assess the role of blockchain technology in moderating the relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management. Building on evidence that blockchain can significantly curb earnings management, we investigate whether firms that have adopted both IFRS and blockchain exhibit higher financial reporting quality than firms that have adopted only IFRS or no innovations. (iii) Third, to provide evidence-based policy implications for regulators, practitioners, and nonfinancial listed companies to increase financial reporting transparency in Vietnam. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: In the next section, we present a summary of the theoretical background and develop the research hypotheses, whereas in section 3, the research methodology is presented. Section 4 reviews the results and discusses the empirical findings. Finally, section 5 concludes and outlines the contributions of the study. 2. Theoretical framework and hypothesis development 2.1. Theoretical foundations 2.1.1. Agency theory Agency theory focuses on the relationship between a principal and an agent, wherein the principal (such as shareholders or investors) delegates authority to the agent (such as company directors or chief executive officers) to act on their behalf. This theory highlights the potential for conflicts of interest because agents may pursue personal goals that differ from those of the principal, especially when information asymmetry exists. This misalignment leads to agency problems such as earnings management, where managers manipulate financial statements to achieve operational targets, secure bonuses, or present a favorable image to investors (Jensen & Meckling, 1976). Khalil & Simon (2014) applied agency theory to demonstrate that IFRS adoption in Egypt led to a reduction in earnings management due to enhanced monitoring capabilities and information quality. Similarly, Doukakis (2014) examined how IFRS adoption affected both accrual-based and real earnings management across 22 European countries and showed that improved transparency curtailed opportunistic managerial behaviors in certain contexts. In this study, agency theory helps explain why earnings management occurs in listed enterprises in Vietnam. Managers, as agents, may exploit their discretion in accounting choices to manage reported earnings, particularly when monitoring is weak or information is opaque. The adoption of IFRS aims to mitigate these agency problems by imposing stricter, more transparent, and internationally recognized reporting standards, thereby reducing the scope for managerial manipulation and aligning the interests of managers and shareholders. Blockchain technology further reinforces this alignment with a decentralized, immutable ledger for recording transactions. This technological innovation significantly enhances the transparency and traceability of financial data, making it difficult for managers to conceal manipulative actions or alter records ex post. Wang & Kogan (2018) theoretically elaborated on how blockchain-based accounting systems address agency problems by creating an environment where managerial manipulative actions become more detectable. In this study, the moderating impact of blockchain on the relationship between https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 4 IFRS adoption and earnings management can be understood as reducing agency costs: with both IFRS and blockchain, principals have better access to reliable information, and agents are less likely to engage in opportunistic behavior. Thus, agency theory underpins the rationale for investigating how these mechanisms jointly curb earnings management. 2.1.2. Institutional theory Institutional theory posits that organizations operate within a social environment and are subject to rules and norms that shape their structures, strategies, and behaviors. According to this theory, organizations conform to institutional pressures, including regulatory requirements (coercive), professional norms (normative), and the practices of leading organizations (mimetic), to gain legitimacy, stability, and access to resources, even if these changes do not immediately increase efficiency or profitability (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983; Scott, 2008). Albu et al. (2020) used institutional theory to examine how Romania's institutional environment shaped IFRS implementation and reported that the formal adoption of standards without significant institutional support limited their effectiveness in improving reporting quality. Institutional theory is particularly relevant in the Vietnamese context, where the adoption of IFRS and blockchain technology is influenced by both external and internal pressures. The Vietnamese government's IFRS adoption roadmap (Decision No. 345/QD-BTC) represents coercive institutional pressure, compelling listed enterprises to comply with international standards. Concurrently, normative pressures arise from professional bodies, international investors, and audit firms advocating for higher-quality, globally comparable financial reporting. Mimetic pressures may also occur as Vietnamese companies observe and emulate the practices of multinational corporations or firms that have successfully adopted IFRS and digital technologies. In this study, institutional theory helps explain why Vietnamese enterprises are transitioning toward IFRS and blockchain adoption, even when facing implementation challenges. Securing legitimacy in the eyes of regulatory bodies and the international investment community motivates firms to adopt these innovations. Furthermore, the institutional environment can moderate the effectiveness of IFRS and blockchain in curbing earnings management: strong regulatory enforcement and professional support can enhance the impact of these tools, whereas weak institutions may limit their efficacy. By applying institutional theory, we acknowledge the sociopolitical and economic context shaping financial reporting practices in Vietnam. 2.1.3. Information transparency theory Information transparency theory emphasizes that the quality, accessibility, and completeness of disclosed information are crucial for reducing information asymmetry and building trust among stakeholders. High transparency ensures that relevant financial information is available to all interested parties in a timely and understandable manner, thereby limiting opportunities for opportunistic managerial behaviors and enhancing market efficiency (Bushman et al., 2004). Information transparency theory directly informs the mechanisms by which IFRS adoption and blockchain technology are expected to reduce earnings management in Vietnamese enterprises. The IFRS, with its comprehensive disclosure requirements and standardization, aims to improve the clarity, comparability, and reliability of financial statements. This increased transparency makes it more difficult for managers to conceal earnings manipulation and easier for external stakeholders such as investors, auditors, and regulators to detect irregularities. Blockchain technology supports these transparency benefits by providing a real-time, tamper-proof record of financial transactions and accounting entries. The decentralized nature of blockchain ensures that all authorized parties have simultaneous access to the same data, reducing the risk of information asymmetry and subsequent manipulation. Cong et al. (2021) used information transparency theory to analyze how blockchain enhances the reliability of disclosed information and reduces information asymmetry in financial markets. Furthermore, Wang et al. (2019) demonstrated how blockchain implementation in supply chain management improved information transparency and reduced opportunistic behavior through real-time verifiability. In this study, the integration of blockchain into financial reporting systems is hypothesized to amplify the transparency achieved through IFRS adoption, leading to a more pronounced reduction in earnings management. This theoretical perspective justifies the investigation of blockchain as a moderating tool and supports the argument that digital innovation can complement regulatory reforms in promoting financial integrity. 2.2. Hypothesis development 2.2.1. The impact of ifrs’ adoption on earnings management The relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management has been extensively studied in the accounting literature, yielding varied findings across different institutional contexts. The theoretical foundation for this hypothesis rests on the premise that IFRS, as a principles-based set of standards with more comprehensive disclosure requirements, should limit managerial opportunism and enhance financial reporting quality. Several empirical studies provide evidence for a negative relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management. Barth et al. (2008) investigated 21 countries and reported that firms applying IFRS exhibit less earnings management, more timely loss recognition, and more value-relevant accounting information than do firms applying non-U.S. domestic standards. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 5 Furthermore, Zéghal et al. (2011) analyzed French companies and noted a significant decrease in earnings management following mandatory IFRS adoption, particularly for firms with good corporate governance and those reliant on foreign capital. Similarly, research by Houqe et al. (2012) demonstrated that IFRS adoption reduces earnings management, with a more pronounced effect in countries with stronger investor protection mechanisms. Additionally, a study by Bryce et al. (2015) revealed that Australian firms showed improved earnings quality after IFRS adoption, with a reduction in abnormal accruals indicating less earnings management. Likewise, Pelucio-Grecco et al. (2014) documented a reduction in discretionary accruals among Brazilian public companies after IFRS adoption, especially in highly regulated industries such as pharmaceuticals. Moreover, Rahmawati & Putri (2019) showed that in nonfinancial companies listed on the Indonesian Stock Exchange, convergence to IFRS significantly curtailed earnings management practices, implying that stringent reporting standards effectively limited managerial opportunism. Consistent with these studies, Tsalavoutas et al. (2020) concluded that mandatory IFRS adoption led to improvements in earnings quality, particularly in jurisdictions with stronger regulatory frameworks. Despite this positive evidence, other studies suggest limitations and even potential unintended consequences of IFRS adoption. For instance, in the Russian context, IFRS implementation was found to increase earnings management activities, as firms exploited the inherent flexibility in principles-based standards to manipulate discretionary accruals (Malofeeva, 2018). Similar patterns have been observed in several Asian countries, where firms exhibited higher levels of earnings management after IFRS adoption, especially in nations with weaker investor protection and less effective enforcement mechanisms (Chen et al., 2010; Leuz et al., 2003). Chen et al. (2010) also identified a substitution effect in emerging markets: while IFRS adoption reduced real earnings management, it led to an increase in accrual-based earnings management, as managers shifted their strategies to exploit new regulatory loopholes. Studies in France and Brazil reported no significant impact or increase in earnings management post-IFRS, suggesting the critical role of institutional factors such as audit quality, legal enforcement, and cultural attitudes toward compliance (Capkun et al., 2016; Iatridis & Rouvolis, 2010). The diversity of these findings highlights the importance of contextual variables in shaping the impact of IFRS on earnings management. Enforcement mechanisms play a crucial role; countries with robust legal frameworks and strong regulatory oversight, such as Saudi Arabia, have witnessed a more pronounced reduction in earnings manipulation (Aladwey & Diab, 2023), whereas weaker enforcement, as seen in some Asian and Eastern European markets, has undermined IFRS effectiveness (Chen et al., 2010; Malofeeva, 2018). Institutional readiness is another critical factor: advanced governance structures and professional expertise, as seen in Sweden, facilitated a greater decline in earnings management post-IFRS adoption than did countries such as South Korea, where regulatory adjustments lagged (Jeanjean & Stolowy, 2008). The type of IFRS adoption also matters; full adoption tends to yield stronger anti-manipulation effects than modified or partial implementations do, which can introduce discretionary loopholes (Barth et al., 2008). The aforementioned findings suggest that the effectiveness of IFRS in reducing earnings management is context dependent. Adoption alone may not guarantee improved reporting quality unless supported by strong legal enforcement, corporate governance, and auditor independence. In the Vietnamese context, where IFRS is currently being adopted under a phased regulatory roadmap, the institutional environment is still maturing. However, the Vietnamese government has demonstrated a commitment to improving financial transparency and aligning with international standards. Drawing lessons from countries with similar transitional economies, IFRS adoption in Vietnam is anticipated to reduce earnings management. Therefore, based on agency theory and supported by international empirical evidence, we propose the following hypothesis: H1: IFRS adoption has a negative effect on earnings management. 2.2.2. The moderating role of blockchain technology The moderating role of blockchain technology in enhancing the effectiveness of IFRS adoption in curbing earnings management has garnered increasing attention in recent research, although findings remain context-dependent and occasionally conflicting. While blockchain's inherent features, such as decentralization, immutability, and real-time transparency, theoretically complement IFRS objectives by reducing information asymmetry and managerial discretion, empirical evidence varies depending on implementation quality, the institutional environment, and corporate governance structures. Several recent empirical studies provide compelling evidence that blockchain enhances the quality and integrity of financial reporting, particularly in firms operating under complex regulatory environments such as IFRS. For instance, Chang et al. (2019) examined how accounting information systems affect financial reporting quality and reported that advanced digital systems significantly enhance the effectiveness of accounting standards in reducing information asymmetry. Similarly, Dai & Vasarhelyi (2017) and Yermack (2017) developed a conceptual framework explaining how blockchain-based accounting systems can provide real-time, verifiable, and transparent recording of transactions, thereby reducing opportunities for ex post manipulation of accounting information. This technological feature directly addresses a fundamental limitation of traditional financial reporting frameworks, including IFRS—the ability to retrospectively alter accounting records. In addition, Appelbaum & Smith (2018) argued that blockchain implementation creates an immutable audit trail, significantly constraining managerial discretion in financial reporting and thereby enhancing the effectiveness of accounting standards. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 6 Furthermore, Wang & Kogan (2018), Schmitz & Leoni (2019), and Fuller & Markelevich (2020) also show that blockchain's ability to protect the security and integrity of transaction data can support secure and transparent financial reporting systems, which are essential for effective IFRS adoption. When blockchain is properly implemented, it not only improves operational efficiency but also strengthens the monitoring function of external stakeholders. In addition, Liu et al. (2019), Moll & Yigitbasioglu (2019), and Cai et al. (2021) further emphasize that blockchain has the potential to revolutionize corporate governance and financial reporting by providing a distributed, tamper-proof ledger. In such a system, any deviations from IFRS principles are more easily detectable by auditors, regulators, and investors, thereby increasing managerial accountability and reducing earnings manipulation. However, other studies suggest limitations to the blockchain-IFRS interaction. For instance, Zhao et al. (2019) argue that while many organizations adopt blockchain in response to institutional pressures, the actual impact on governance and financial integrity is limited when the technology is poorly integrated or used symbolically. Similarly, Schmitz & Leoni (2019) caution that the potential of blockchain in accounting is often overstated. Their review highlights that many blockchain projects are still in experimental phases and that existing organizational structures may not yet be ready to support their full potential in improving earnings quality. They argue that blockchain benefits can be realized only when firms adopt robust governance frameworks and invest in employee training and technological infrastructure. Coyne & McMickle (2017) also warned that while blockchain promises improved auditability and transparency, its actual impact depends on organizational readiness, system integration, and data standardization. Without these factors, blockchain may have little impact on earnings management, even with IFRS in place. Additionally, an analysis of U.S. supply chains (2024) revealed that supplier firms increased earnings management after their customers adopted blockchain due to heightened market expectations and reduced external monitoring (Smith & Lee, 2024). Similarly, modified IFRS implementation in Indonesia showed no significant improvement in financial transparency when combined with blockchain because local adjustments introduced discretionary loopholes. These results indicate that blockchain effectiveness depends on its integration depth and regulatory environment. For example, superficial blockchain adoption— limited to specific departments rather than enterprise-wide systems—may not enhance the impact of IFRS. Overall, studies suggest that blockchain technology can play a moderating role in strengthening the negative relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management, but only under certain conditions. When blockchain is effectively implemented and integrated into financial reporting systems, it reinforces the enforceability and transparency of IFRS, making it more difficult for managers to engage in earnings manipulation. However, this moderating effect is not automatic and may be absent in firms with weak technological infrastructure or tokenistic adoption. In the Vietnamese context, where both IFRS adoption and blockchain technology implementation are in their early stages, it becomes essential to examine whether nonfinancial listed companies adopting blockchain experience a greater reduction in earnings management under IFRS. Therefore, we propose the following hypothesis: H2: Blockchain technology adoption moderates the relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management such that the negative relationship is stronger in firms with higher levels of blockchain adoption. Methodology In this study, we employ a quantitative, cross-sectional research design to examine the relationships among IFRS adoption, blockchain technology implementation, and earnings management in nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam. We utilize both primary and secondary data in our research model. Primary data were collected through structured questionnaires to capture detailed information about IFRS implementation processes and blockchain technology adoption that is not available in published financial reports. Secondary financial data were gathered from companies' audited annual reports to provide objective metrics for calculating earnings management proxies and control variables. The target population for this study comprises all nonfinancial enterprises listed on Vietnam's two main stock exchanges: the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange (HOSE) and the Hanoi Stock Exchange (HNX). As of December 2024, this population included approximately 672 companies after financial institutions (banks, insurance companies, and financial services firms) were excluded because their distinct regulatory requirements and reporting practices could complicate the analysis of earnings management. A sample of 240 nonfinancial listed companies was selected for this study; the final sample consisted of 218 valid responses from the 240 targeted companies. The respondents among the 218 sampled companies included the following: chief financial officers (CFOs): 98 respondents (45.0%); financial controllers: 69 respondents (31.7%); chief accountants: 40 respondents (18.3%); and finance/accounting directors: 11 respondents (5%). These individuals were targeted because they possess comprehensive knowledge of both financial reporting practices and technology implementation within their organizations. All respondents had at least 5 years of experience in their current roles and were directly involved in financial reporting decisions, ensuring that they had the necessary expertise to provide reliable feedback on IFRS adoption and blockchain implementation. The study used a stratified random sampling technique based on both industry classification and company size to ensure representativeness across different sectors and scales. For industry stratification, companies were categorized into nine nonfinancial industries on the basis of the Vietnam Standard Industrial Classification (VSIC) system. For size stratification, companies were classified on the basis of their market capitalization as of December 31, 2024. Primary data were collected through structured questionnaires administered to the chief financial officers (CFOs), financial controllers, chief accountants, and senior finance/accounting directors of the 218 sampled companies from February to May 2025. The questionnaire was designed on the basis of established instruments from prior research, adapted to the Vietnamese context, and refined through a pilot study with 10 CFOs and 2 academics specializing in accounting research and teaching. This study employed snowball sampling for questionnaire distribution, which was carried out through both online and in-person platforms. The online surveys were hosted via Google Forms. Personalized emails were sent to the official email addresses of the surveyed individuals, which were obtained from company websites, annual reports, and official stock exchange listings. Each email contained a unique survey link to track responses and prevent duplicate submissions. In-person surveys were conducted at companies headquartered in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi and at seminars and investment forums organized by the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) in April 2025 in Hanoi. Secondary data for calculating earnings management and control variables were collected over a three-year period (2022-2024) to allow for a more robust calculation of discretionary accruals and to control for potential year-specific anomalies. Compared with single-year data, this approach provides a more reliable measure of earnings management activities (DeFond & Subramanyam, 1998). Financial data were extracted from multiple sources to ensure comprehensiveness and accuracy: audited financial statements from the annual reports of the sampled companies for the fiscal years 2022, 2023, and 2024, accessed via the companies' official websites; the State Securities Commission of Vietnam (SSC) information disclosure system; and the Vietstock.vn website. Discussion The negative relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management aligns with several influential studies in the accounting literature. Barth et al. (2008) reported that firms adopting IFRSs presented less earnings management than did those using local standards across 21 countries. Similarly, Zéghal et al. (2011) reported that mandatory IFRS adoption in France led to reduced earnings management among listed companies. Our findings also complement those of Chen et al. (2010), who demonstrated improved accounting quality, including reduced earnings management, following IFRS adoption in European Union countries. The direct effect of blockchain technology on earnings management supports the theoretical propositions of Dai & Vasarhelyi (2017), who argued that blockchain's immutable recording capabilities would enhance accounting transparency and reduce manipulation opportunities. Our empirical evidence validates these theoretical predictions. Similarly, the findings align with those of Schmitz & Leoni (2019), who suggested that blockchain technology reduces information asymmetry between preparers and users of financial information, thereby constraining managerial discretion in financial reporting. The moderating effect of blockchain technology on the IFRS-earnings management relationship represents our study's most novel contribution, extending Gao et al. (2020) theoretical framework. While they proposed potential synergies between blockchain and accounting standards conceptually, our study provides empirical evidence of this interaction. Our findings also complement Wang & Kogan's (2018) work on blockchain-based transaction processing systems by demonstrating how such systems interact with accounting standards to enhance reporting integrity. However, our findings diverge from those of several previous studies. Ahmed et al. (2013) reported increased earnings management after mandatory IFRS adoption across 20 countries, contradicting our results. This discrepancy likely stems from contextual differences: our study examines voluntary IFRS adoption in Vietnam, whereas they focused on mandatory adoption across diverse jurisdictions. Firms that voluntarily adopt IFRS may be inherently more committed to transparency and better governance, explaining the different outcomes. The Vietnamese regulatory environment's gradual approach to IFRS implementation may also allow firms to develop the necessary expertise and systems before full compliance, potentially leading to better implementation quality. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 12 Our results contrast with those of Jeanjean & Stolowy (2008), who reported no significant decline in earnings management following IFRS adoption in Australia, France, or the UK. This difference may be attributed to temporal factors: their study examined the initial IFRS implementation period (2005--2006), whereas our research reflects more contemporary IFRS implementation with refined standards and accumulated implementation experience. Additionally, emerging economies such as Vietnam may experience more pronounced benefits from IFRS adoption than developed markets with already sophisticated accounting systems do. With respect to blockchain technology, our finding of its significant moderating effect differs from studies such as Cai (2021), who positioned blockchain primarily as having direct effects on reporting quality. Our results suggest a more complex relationship where blockchain influence extends beyond direct effects to conditioning the effectiveness of accounting standards themselves. This interaction effect represents a novel contribution to the literature on financial technology in accounting contexts. 6. Conclusions and contributions To address our hypotheses, we first conducted a comprehensive literature review examining the underlying theories of agency and institutional perspectives on financial reporting quality. We analyzed the theoretical frameworks connecting IFRS adoption with earnings management constraints and integrated the emerging blockchain literature to develop a conceptual model of technology‒standard interactions. Second, we collected insights from financial managers and accounting professionals across various Vietnamese industries through preliminary interviews that informed our survey instrument development and validated the contextual relevance of our hypothesized relationships. Finally, we perform hierarchical regression analysis on a sample of 218 nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam, specifically companies listed on the Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi stock exchanges that have been operating for 5 years or more. This analysis tested both the direct effect of IFRS adoption on earnings management and the moderating effect of blockchain technology adoption on this relationship. On the basis of these steps, we draw the following conclusions. First, IFRS adoption has a significant negative association with earnings management practices, suggesting that even the voluntary implementation of international standards constrains opportunistic reporting behaviors in the Vietnamese market. Second, blockchain technology adoption not only directly reduces earnings management but also significantly enhances the effectiveness of IFRS implementation, as evidenced by the significant negative interaction term in our model. Most notably, the relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management becomes nonsignificant at low blockchain adoption levels, indicating that technological infrastructure may be a necessary condition for accounting standards to effectively constrain earnings manipulation. Theoretically, this research has proven the existence of a significant interaction effect between accounting standard implementation and technological infrastructure in determining financial reporting quality. The empirical evidence demonstrates that blockchain technology adoption significantly moderates the relationship between IFRS adoption and earnings management practices, with the negative association becoming stronger at higher levels of blockchain implementation. This finding advances the accounting literature by challenging the conventional approach that examines accounting standards and technology adoption as separate domains with independent effects on reporting outcomes. Instead, our results support an integrated theoretical framework where regulatory mechanisms and technological infrastructure function as complementary rather than substitutive governance tools. This interaction effect extends agency theory by identifying how the combined implementation of standards and technology creates synergistic constraints on managerial opportunism through a multilayered reduction in information asymmetry. The contingent nature of IFRS effectiveness on technological readiness also provides a potential explanation for inconsistent findings in the prior literature regarding standard adoption outcomes across different jurisdictions and time periods. Our research establishes that the institutional context, particularly technological infrastructure, conditions the efficacy of accounting standards in achieving their intended outcomes. In practice, the results of this research will support managers at nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam in realizing the importance of coordinated investments in both accounting standard implementation and blockchain technology adoption. The significant moderating effect indicates that firms focusing exclusively on IFRS compliance without corresponding technological infrastructure may achieve suboptimal financial reporting quality improvements. Strategic resource allocation should therefore consider these complementary relationships to maximize returns on financial reporting investments and enhance market credibility. In addition, the research also significantly supports policy makers in Vietnam by providing empirical evidence that technological readiness should be incorporated into IFRS implementation roadmaps. As Vietnam progresses toward mandatory IFRS adoption, regulatory bodies should consider developing parallel initiatives to enhance technological infrastructure, particularly blockchain capabilities, within the corporate sector. Although this study has achieved significant findings regarding the moderating effect of blockchain technology on the IFRS-earnings management relationship, the research is still limited by its cross-sectional design, which prevents causal inferences and examination of how these relationships evolve over time as both IFRS and blockchain implementations mature in the Vietnamese market. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 13 Ethical considerations The study strictly adhered to ethical principles for research involving human subjects. JSON: Name: ifrs_blockchain_earnings_vn Title: Hierarchical regression analysis of the moderating effect of blockchain adoption on the impact of IFRS adoption on earnings management in Vietnamese nonfinancial listed companies Short Hypothesis: Higher levels of IFRS adoption cause lower earnings management, and this negative effect is amplified in firms with greater blockchain technology adoption. Related Work: Existing research evaluates the IFRS→earnings-management link primarily via archival accrual-based measures (modified Jones and performance-matched models) and reports heterogeneous outcomes across jurisdictions: reductions in discretionary accruals in settings with strong enforcement, null or increased accrual manipulation where enforcement is weak, and potential substitution toward real activities manipulation. Separately, blockchain literature is mostly conceptual or case-based, arguing immutability and traceability can improve reporting quality; a few empirical studies examine direct blockchain adoption effects but rely on proxies or limited samples. Common methodological weaknesses across prior work include reliance on single-source archival proxies for institutional and technology adoption, cross-sectional or short-window designs that limit causal claims, limited controls for endogeneity and managerial selection into adoption, inconsistent measurement of technology depth (tokenistic vs integrated adoption), and scarce evidence combining regulatory adoption measures with direct firm-level technology adoption metrics in emerging markets. These gaps leave unresolved whether and how blockchain conditions the IFRS→earnings-management relationship in contexts with evolving enforcement. Abstract: This research evaluates whether IFRS adoption reduces earnings management and whether blockchain adoption strengthens that effect in Vietnamese nonfinancial listed firms. Using firm-level survey measures of IFRS and blockchain implementation combined with three-year audited financials (2022–2024), the study applies hierarchical regression with an interaction term to test moderation effects on absolute discretionary accruals (modified Jones/performance-matched measures). The principal contribution is an integrated, firm-level test of regulatory standard implementation and distributed ledger technology, using direct measures of both constructs rather than proxies. Expected outcomes are (1) a negative coefficient on IFRS adoption indicating reduced accrual-based earnings management, (2) an independent negative effect of blockchain adoption, and (3) a significant negative interaction term showing that blockchain amplifies IFRS effectiveness. Results will clarify whether technological infrastructure is a necessary complement to accounting-standard reform for improving reporting quality in emerging markets. Experiments: Datasets: sample of nonfinancial companies listed on HOSE and HNX with complete audited financial statements for 2022–2024 and matched primary-survey responses from CFOs/chief accountants (target N≈218). Construct earnings-management dependent variables: (a) absolute discretionary accruals (|DA|) via modified Jones model, (b) performance-matched discretionary accruals (Kothari et al. adjustment), and (c) alternative DA measures for robustness. Key independent variables: firm-level IFRS adoption score (4-item Likert composite) and blockchain adoption score (4-item Likert composite) from surveys. Controls: ln(total assets), leverage (avg debt/assets 2022–24), ROA (avg 2022–24), Big-Four audit dummy, ownership concentration, growth rate, firm age, and industry dummies (8). Baselines: (1) OLS regression with controls only; (2) OLS with IFRS only; (3) OLS with IFRS and blockchain main effects; (4) hierarchical model adding IFRS×blockchain interaction. Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates, robust (HC) standard errors, p-values, adjusted R2, ∆R2 for nested models, standardized beta, variance inflation factors (VIF). Statistical tests: t-tests for coefficients, F-test for model change, simple-slope analysis at ±1 SD of moderator, and Johnson–Neyman region-of-significance. Robustness and ablation studies: (A) substitute DA specification (performance-matched) to test sensitivity; (B) remove each control set (audit, ownership, industry) sequentially to evaluate coefficient stability; (C) split-sample analysis by blockchain adoption (top tertile vs bottom tertile) and by voluntary vs early IFRS adopters; (D) propensity-score matching on observables to compare adopters vs non-adopters and estimate average treatment effect on |DA|; (E) instrumental-variable (IV) regression where feasible using exogenous proxies for blockchain exposure (e.g., regional digital infrastructure index) to probe endogeneity; (F) bootstrap (1,000 replications) to obtain confidence intervals for interaction effect. Implementation details: use heteroskedasticity-robust OLS, report VIFs, cluster SEs by industry if intra-industry correlation present, and report full model diagnostics (residual plots, influence/leverage). Thresholds: significance at conventional levels (0.10/0.05/0.01). Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error and self-report bias in survey-based IFRS and blockchain scores; potential reverse causality and selection bias (firms with lower earnings management may be more likely to adopt IFRS/blockchain); omitted variable bias from unobserved governance or IT-capability factors; limited sample size (≈218) reducing power for IV and subgroup analyses and restricting detection of small effects; cross-sectional design (even with three-year financial windows) prevents definitive causal inference and temporal dynamics assessment; blockchain adoption may be superficial (tokenistic) leading to overestimation or underestimation of true effect; external validity limited to Vietnamese nonfinancial listed firms and to voluntary-adoption context; multicollinearity between IFRS and blockchain measures could inflate standard errors; reliance on accrual-based earnings-management proxies misses real activities manipulation substitution; potential survey non-response and survivorship biases in the listed-firm sample; limited capacity to find valid, strong instruments for IV identification; model sensitivity to specification choices and industry heterogeneity.
